subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Sarika, it's Sachin, and I have to say this out loud once. In the corridor before assembly, Nikhil and his group kept grabbing my bag and throwing it around, calling me names. There were maybe thirty people there. Some stared at their phones, some looked at the floor, and two laughed. Not one said stop. That silence felt worse than the names. I felt like a piece of furniture. You were the only one who found me at the water tap, and you did not ask anything, you just sat there. Then you said, "Come with me to the counsellor." She listened, said it was not my fault, and called my class teacher and my family that same afternoon.

qa.q: About how many people were in the corridor?
qa.a: There were maybe thirty people in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did the silence feel worse than the names to Sachin?
qa.a: The silence made Sachin feel alone and invisible, like a piece of furniture, as if nobody saw the harm as real.

qa.q: What turning point helped Sachin that day?
qa.a: Sarika sat quietly at the water tap and then took Sachin to the counsellor, who listened, said it was not Sachin's fault, and called the class teacher and family that afternoon.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling when finding Sachin at the water tap and sitting without asking anything?
qa.a: Sarika probably felt concerned and unsure what to say, and chose company over questions so that Sachin would not feel pushed.

grounding: A student being harassed notices that many people see it and nobody speaks; the silence hurts, and an adult responds the same day.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: My name is Chandrika, and I saw it on the school bus home. Two boys in the back seat kept flicking paper balls at Sangeeta and calling out about her hair. The bus was full, maybe twenty-five of us. Nobody said a word. A few people put in earphones and turned to the window. Sangeeta pressed her forehead to the glass and hugged her bag, and her shoulders shrank a little more at every stop. I felt frozen in my seat too. At the market stop I made myself stand up, sat down beside her and called Mrs Rao, the bus attendant, to the back. Mrs Rao moved the boys to the front, stayed near Sangeeta for the rest of the ride and phoned the principal, who said the boys' families would be called that evening. Sangeeta did not say much, but she let me keep the seat.

qa.q: Where did the boys pick on Sangeeta?
qa.a: On the school bus home, where two boys in the back seat flicked paper balls at Sangeeta and called out about her hair.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been feeling with her forehead pressed to the glass?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably humiliated and alone; hugging her bag and shrinking at every stop suggests the silence of the full bus hurt as much as the boys' words.

qa.q: What turning point came at the market stop?
qa.a: Chandrika stood up, sat beside Sangeeta and called Mrs Rao, who moved the boys, stayed near Sangeeta and phoned the principal.

qa.q: What was it like for Chandrika to sit frozen while the paper balls kept flying?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to have felt stuck and uneasy, part of the silent crowd, until standing up broke that silence.

grounding: A student being picked on sees a whole bus watch in silence, and a fellow passenger's account shows how that silence isolates her until someone steps in and adults respond the same day.
